title: Another HORRIBLE Bodybuilding Program (HYPERMASS by Noel Deyzel)
summary: He reviews Noel Deyzel's 8-week Hypermass program and rates it terrible for natural novices. His complaints: a fixed short timeline, a 5-6 meals/day rule, a tempo gimmick on every lift, huge volumes of light isolation work, high-rep deadlifts and squats, and compounds placed after pre-fatiguing isolation. Ironically, the optional arm and calf/abs days are the best parts.
claims: A bodybuilding program with a fixed timeline (here 8 weeks) is a red flag; a novice program should run until progress stalls
Fixed short programs encourage novices to program-hop, a major reason many never progress
Novices don't need 5-6 meals a day; eat 2-3 times as usual and calories rise naturally
As a novice he gained weight just by adding an extra bowl of rice a day
Making beginners live a pro bodybuilder's draconian lifestyle makes them burn out before seeing results
In his pyramid of hypertrophy, intensity, volume and frequency sit at the top; tempo is near the bottom for naturals
Prescribing strict tempos like 4-0-1-0 on every lift forces lighter weights, slows progression and confuses novices; it suits only very advanced lifters
Use slow controlled negatives to keep form and tightness and lengthen the muscle, then explode up, but never time them
Opening a back day with 4x20 lat pulldowns is aerobics with weights; machine/cable isolation belongs at the end after heavy compounds
His upper back was built by heavy deadlifts, rows and pull-ups; cable isolation alone doesn't give enough tonnage
10-rep deadlift sets are too high for novices; poor stimulus-to-fatigue ratio and they burn out
4-second negatives on deadlifts will wreck a novice's core and form within three reps; use Romanian deadlifts for an eccentric focus
15 seconds of rest between sets with a challenging weight isn't enough to recover; it turns training into cardio
Hundreds of low-intensity reps per session create bored lifters who text in the gym
Huge bicep volume (13+ sets in one session) is bro-pump training and a waste of time; he never needed that much
Novices should train 45 minutes to an hour at most, not 2.5-3 hours
Growth comes from a select number of intense sets, then rest and recovery, not from working a muscle as much as possible
Drop sets on the first exercise make no sense for novices; use standard straight sets and get fancy only once the basics are down
On a once-a-week chest day, the chest is done after about two exercises with real weights; extra exercises add fatigue without stimulus
Calves need high frequency spread across the week; 4-8 sets once a week just makes you sore; small calves are usually bad training, not genetics
Supersetting curls with skull crushers is a great arm pairing; an arm day should be low stress, the one you look forward to
Compound movements are essential; good novice programs are mostly compounds with isolation added
4x20 back squats (widowmaker style) gas novices out and make them hate squats; 4 sets of 3-5 would be far better
Lying hamstring curls on leg day stretch the hamstrings and help prevent injury, but drop-setting to 30 reps is unnecessary for novices
For unilateral movements like walking lunges he prefers higher reps and lower intensity, e.g. 4x20
Most YouTuber programs become decent once you cut about 60% of the gimmicks
Lower body days should be short and upper body days longer, because legs move more tonnage
Glute cable kickbacks are unnecessary; the guys he knows built big glutes strictly from squats and deadlifts and he has never done one
Stay in the gym until muscular endurance or mental stamina runs out; most novices have little mental stamina
Copying IFBB pros is a bad idea for naturals because they are on drugs
Opening a shoulder day with 10x10 lateral raises pre-fatigues for nothing; start with a heavy compound press when you are freshest
Naturals with big delts mostly credit pressing; isolation does something but barely
Add volume with caution: a little goes a long way and it's easy to overdo
After 15 years of training he couldn't survive this volume except by sandbagging every set, which is what novices will end up doing
Putting presses and close-grip bench at the end, after all the isolation, is backwards scheduling
Putting calves and abs at the end of a program means people skip them
Pullovers are the most underrated exercise; 4x12 is the right way to do them
Warm up with the main exercise at lighter weight, not leg extension isolation
A novice doing 3x5 squats twice a week has plenty of leg volume
Supersets should usually pair antagonists to save time; supersetting the same muscle or two compounds (leg press + hack squat) is rarely justified
